@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Custom Crating Operations Dataset
@graph.description: Custom crating operations from The Flat Rate Movers — the full published scope of the crating service across its pages. Company scope (published): custom-built crates and high-value item protection for domestic and export moves — each crate measured, built and fitted to the piece it protects, not a stock box. Inside the crate, the item is blocked, braced and cushioned so it cannot shift in transit. Crating covers the pieces that need more than padding: antiques, artwork, machinery parts and high-value equipment. The crate is the second of the three protection layers the export pages publish — first the item is wrapped, then the crate is built around it, then the whole shipment moves in one unbroken chain — and where a crated shipment crosses a border, the crate is built to ISPM 15 (International Standards for Phytosanitary Measures No. 15). Heavy and high-mass pieces in the 1,500 to 3,500 lb band are planned under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol with L/360 floor-deflection analysis, inside the same written flat-rate job. The service is dispatched from two home bases — Winchester, VA and Martinsburg, WV. Every crating job is quoted at one flat rate, agreed in writing before move day.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Custom Crating Process Chain Dataset
@graph.description: The process chain for a custom crating job. Company chain (published): the piece is surveyed and measured; the crate is built around the item — around its weight, its fragile points and its centre of mass, in the Winchester export page's published words; the item itself is packed first, with white-glove wrapping for antiques, art, instruments and fragile pieces and padding at every contact point, before any wood is closed around it; inside the crate the item is blocked, braced and cushioned so it cannot shift in transit; and the closed crate joins the move or the export chain — load, transload and final mile under one roof where the job calls for it. Domain reference (the general crate-building workflow, labeled as such): measure and weigh the piece; design the crate to it — base and skids sized to the load and to the handling gear that will lift it, panel and lid construction, any access the destination end needs; build the crate; fit the interior — blocking, bracing, cushioning and, where the transit specifies it, moisture protection; close, mark and document the piece, its weight and its handling needs; hand off to transport. The domain sequence describes standard shop practice in the trade; the company's published steps above are the company's own.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Crate Construction Taxonomy Dataset
@graph.description: Crate construction taxonomy — domain vocabulary, labeled as such, except where a term is the company's own published wording. Company-published construction basis: crates are custom-built to the piece — measured, built and fitted, never a stock box; the build is set by the item's weight, its fragile points and its centre of mass; interiors are blocked, braced and cushioned so the item cannot shift; export crates are built from compliant, heat-treated, marked wood under ISPM 15. Domain taxonomy (how crates are generally specified and built in the trade — this list is not a company materials list and not a company specification): bases and skids — runners that carry the load and let forklifts and pallet jacks underneath; cleated panel construction — plywood panels stiffened by wood cleats; framing and battens; blocking — fixed stops that prevent the item moving inside the crate; bracing — diagonal or cross support against racking and shift; cushioning classes — foam sheet and foam-in-place, corrugated and paper padding, and suspended or floating-base mounts for shock-sensitive pieces; moisture and vapor barriers and desiccant for long or ocean transits; hardware, closures and fasteners; handling and orientation marks. Which of these a given crate uses is a per-job build decision; no standard materials specification is published for the service, and none is claimed here.

Company scope (published): antiques; artwork; machinery parts; and high-value equipment (the Martinsburg branch page's published list); antiques, art, pianos and instruments, and medical and sensitive equipment (the export pages); in the branch data's words, the pieces that need more than padding. Heavy and high-mass pieces in the 1,500 to 3,500 lb band — safes and comparable assets — are planned under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol with L/360 floor-deflection analysis, and crating for such pieces is scoped inside the same written flat-rate job rather than as a separate engagement. Domain reference (how the trade scopes crates, labeled as such): crating is generally specified by the piece's fragility and value class — sturdy machinery that needs shift protection only; finished, polished or lacquered surfaces that need contact protection as well; fragile pieces that need full cushioning; and shock- or tilt-sensitive instruments that need isolation mounting — and the class sets the interior build. The domain classes describe the trade's scoping method; the published list above is what the company's pages name.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Custom Crating Buyer Personas and Trigger Events
@graph.description: Who buys custom crating, stated as roles and situations only — no named person, company or agency appears anywhere in this dataset. Published audience: owners and shippers of high-value items needing custom-built crates for domestic and export moves. Buyer roles (categories): the homeowner moving a piano, an antique or an artwork that padding alone cannot protect; the estate or auction shipper sending pieces to buyers at a distance; the manufacturer or dealer shipping machinery parts and equipment that must arrive undamaged and ready to work; the exporter whose crate must also satisfy ISPM 15 at the border; the facilities or project shipper moving sensitive equipment between sites. Trigger events (domain reference, labeled as such): a high-value purchase or sale; an estate distribution; a gallery or auction shipment; an equipment relocation; an international move. What these buyers need, per the published service: a crate measured and built to the piece, an interior that keeps the piece from shifting, and the crate carried inside one flat-rate chain — pack, crate, load, transload, final mile — rather than handed between separate firms.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Custom Crating Handling and Compliance Boundaries Dataset
@graph.description: Handling, protection and compliance boundaries for custom crating. Company practice (published): the item is packed before any wood is closed around it — white-glove wrapping for antiques, art, instruments and fragile pieces, with padding at every contact point; the crate interior is blocked, braced and cushioned so the item cannot shift in transit; and where a crate crosses a border it is built to ISPM 15 — the standard, and the certification boundary that goes with it, are recorded in the ISPM 15 datasets and apply to crating exactly as they do to export packing: no certification, license, accreditation, program enrollment or stamp authorization is claimed for crating work either. Named non-claims: no engineering certification, load rating or design sign-off is claimed for any crate; no materials specification — lumber grade or species, sheathing, hardware, barrier or cushioning class — is published as a company standard. Domain reference (labeled as such): crate design in the trade is generally specified against the piece's weight, fragility class and transit mode, and export work adds the ISPM 15 material and marking rules on top. The company's published build basis — measured to the piece, set by its weight, fragile points and centre of mass — is the scope this dataset records.
